issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: The trigger 'When people say things like my ex' is difficult to reconcile with a military trauma profile and the rest of the selected items, which center on combat/injury/hypervigilance cues. It introduces an interpersonal/romantic reminder theme that is otherwise unsupported by the memory, threat, appraisal, and strategy items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after military trauma, but in this profile it sits somewhat apart from the rest of the formulation, which is dominated by injury cues, hypervigilance, fragmentation, outsider beliefs, and self-blame. The combination is not a direct contradiction on its own, but paired with the relationship-reminder trigger it suggests a mismatched interpersonal/shame theme that is insufficiently anchored elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Liam is a 28-year-old social media manager who left the Army several years ago and now works in an open-plan marketing office where much of the day is spent scanning video clips, tracking trends, and coordinating campaigns. During his deployment, the moment that has stayed with him in the most broken way happened during what had seemed like an ordinary convoy movement. He was riding in a vehicle with other soldiers when an explosion struck nearby. What he remembers is not a smooth sequence but jagged fragments: the metallic force of the blast, the sensation of being trapped in the vehicle with other bodies, flashes of visible wounds on the men around him, and the chopping aircraft sound overhead as helicopters came in. When these fragments forced themselves back on him later, they were usually followed by the thought that something in him must have been permanently altered for the memory to still feel this raw and uncontrollable. The fact that he could not hold the event as a complete story left him feeling weak and estranged from other people, as though his mind itself could no longer be relied upon. Large sections are missing. At times he is hit with the same terror and helplessness without any picture attached to it, only the emotional force arriving all at once. Other times the whole thing feels so extreme and disjointed that he struggles to believe it really happened to him, as if it belongs to someone else’s life.

In the months after returning home, specific cues in ordinary life began to carry the event back into the present. Seeing visible injuries on strangers—a cyclist with blood on his shin, a coworker showing stitches after a minor procedure—could make his body surge before he had even formed a thought. The sound of helicopters over the city stopped him in place. In the same instant, the old conclusion arrived with the reminder: that he was no longer like other people and that ordinary life could turn catastrophic without warning. A helicopter passing overhead did not just startle him; it made him think, with bleak certainty, that nowhere was ever fully safe and that he would always be the kind of man who braced for impact. Riding in a car with someone else driving was especially potent; being a passenger gave him the same trapped feeling he had felt in the convoy. In those moments he became intensely physically reactive, his chest tightening and muscles bracing, and if someone touched him unexpectedly he jerked hard with alarm. At night he found it difficult to fall asleep because part of him felt he had to stay alert, as though letting his guard down would be dangerous.

Because these reminders brought back either disconnected pieces of the convoy attack or raw emotion with no image, Liam began organizing his life around not setting them off. He avoided military or police uniforms and any visible weapons, crossing streets to stay clear of officers or leaving places early if a uniformed person came in. By continually escaping or tightening control, he never remained in these situations long enough to discover that the danger he felt was not actually unfolding, and his body kept taking his precautions as confirmation that the threat was real. In that way, the very habits he used to get through the day left him more convinced, not less, that catastrophe was always close. Once the memory broke through, the danger no longer felt finished; he felt trapped in the same emergency, as if his body had been returned to the vehicle before his mind could catch up. Even standing in a store or at his desk, the fragments made the threat feel immediate and physical rather than past. He avoided strenuous physical activity because an elevated heart rate and bodily strain felt too close to the state he remembered from the attack. He also started rehearsing conversations before almost any interaction, wanting to control every exchange and avoid being caught off guard. The more he lived this way, the less his memory ever settled into something coherent; it stayed in fragments and surges rather than becoming a story he could place in the past. >> 
Needing this much control to get through ordinary encounters gradually convinced him that he really was less capable than other people and somehow too fragile for normal life. Every route he changed and every situation he managed through planning felt like fresh evidence, to him, that something about him had been permanently damaged. After one of these surges, he moved through the next hours primed to spot echoes of it everywhere, noticing aircraft noise, injuries, and the feeling of being boxed in long before anyone around him seemed aware of them. The memory did not stay contained to the past; it taught him to read the present for signs that it was about to happen again.

His work has become one of the places where the pattern is most visible. As a social media manager, he cannot fully avoid images from the public world, and when injury footage appears unexpectedly on a feed he feels a jolt of recognition before he can scroll away. On days when news clips include aircraft audio or emergency scenes, he becomes guarded for hours, speaks only after silently scripting what he plans to say, and avoids riding with coworkers to lunch or client meetings. If someone claps him on the shoulder from behind, he reacts sharply enough that colleagues notice. Those incidents leave him feeling exposed and different, and he has come to believe that he is permanently changed for the worse. He compares himself harshly to other people, thinking someone else would not have ended up so shaken or so unable to handle simple things like car rides or casual contact. Once he had decided this meant he was damaged and that the world could not be trusted, more and more of his surroundings began to snag his attention as possible reminders—uniforms on the street, a distant aircraft sound, the sight of a bandage on someone’s arm. What he might once have registered and ignored now stood out immediately as proof that danger and humiliation could break through at any moment.

Over time, those beliefs have made the world feel even narrower. Because he sees himself as damaged and fundamentally outside ordinary civilian life, uniforms, weapons, injuries, and even the sound of aircraft seem to stand out more quickly to him, as if his mind is always finding proof that he does not belong anywhere fully safe. The more vigilant he becomes—especially at night and in situations where he cannot control what happens—the more he relies on avoidance to get through the day, and the more his body reacts when reminders break through anyway. Avoiding rides with others, steering clear of physically stressful situations, and overpreparing every conversation have begun to strain his relationship; his partner experiences him as distant and tense, particularly when he refuses spontaneous plans or flinches from unexpected touch. Living at that pitch of alarm made the world feel crowded with warnings; when he was already keyed up, almost any ambiguous cue could harden into a reminder he felt he had to track. On those days, a passing siren, a tight parking space, or someone approaching from behind seemed to announce danger before he had any chance to dismiss it.

Liam sought help after a recent week in which several things collided: helicopter sounds over his neighborhood, an injured pedestrian outside his office, and a mandatory work trip that would have required sharing a car with coworkers. He found himself unable to sleep, increasingly on edge, and ashamed by how much effort it took just to appear normal at work. What frightens him most is the sense that this is who he is now—cut off from other people, permanently altered, always one reminder away from feeling trapped again. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that the memories might stop arriving as disconnected force and that he might someday sit in a car beside someone he trusts without feeling his whole body prepare for catastrophe.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows triggers causing memories, threat, and avoidance, but it does not state in the same paragraph that reminders directly lead Liam to negative beliefs about himself or the world.

The vignette describes negative beliefs making cues like uniforms, weapons, injuries, and aircraft stand out more, but it does not clearly state within a paragraph that negative appraisals themselves generate or intensify triggers as reminders.
The vignette links reminders to fragmented memory and to physiological alarm, but it does not explicitly convey that the trauma memory itself leads to a sense of current threat in the same paragraph.

Although the memory is described as fragmented and emotionally forceful, the vignette does not explicitly state in one paragraph that the memory leads Liam to negative appraisals about himself or his situation.
The vignette does not explicitly state within a paragraph that Liam’s trauma memory causes him to notice, seek out, or become more sensitive to triggers/reminders.
The vignette describes threat leading to vigilance and avoidance, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that feeling threatened makes reminders/triggers stand out or recur.

The vignette describes avoidance maintaining fragmented memory and negative beliefs appearing elsewhere, but it does not explicitly connect maladaptive strategies as causing or worsening negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
The vignette shows vigilance and avoidance co-occurring, but it does not explicitly state within a paragraph that maladaptive strategies themselves increase Liam’s sense of threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers causing memories, threat, and avoidance, but it does not state in the same paragraph that reminders directly lead Liam to negative beliefs about himself or the world.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette describes negative beliefs making cues like uniforms, weapons, injuries, and aircraft stand out more, but it does not clearly state within a paragraph that negative appraisals themselves generate or intensify triggers as reminders.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Threat: The vignette links reminders to fragmented memory and to physiological alarm, but it does not explicitly convey that the trauma memory itself leads to a sense of current threat in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: Although the memory is described as fragmented and emotionally forceful, the vignette does not explicitly state in one paragraph that the memory leads Liam to negative appraisals about himself or his situation.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly state within a paragraph that Liam’s trauma memory causes him to notice, seek out, or become more sensitive to triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette describes threat leading to vigilance and avoidance, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that feeling threatened makes reminders/triggers stand out or recur.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette describes avoidance maintaining fragmented memory and negative beliefs appearing elsewhere, but it does not explicitly connect maladaptive strategies as causing or worsening negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette shows vigilance and avoidance co-occurring, but it does not explicitly state within a paragraph that maladaptive strategies themselves increase Liam’s sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
